header:
Meeting: EvalOps regression hypothesis review
Date/Time: 2026-12-09 16:00 PST
Duration: 54 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luca Ortiz (Redwood SE), Jordan Park (Redwood Solutions Eng); Priya Das (Head of ML - Talon), Evan Murray (Platform), Sofia Alvarez (Product), Aaron Li (Data)
Recording ID: ff-2026-12-09-talon-regression-1a2b3c
summary: Redwood team demo'd Eval/Quality monitoring features focusing on prompt-set based regression alerts, A/B compare flows, and how the Console + Optimize recommendations reduce cost while maintaining quality. Customer is interested in running a short pilot with canonical prompts to validate drift/regression detection against production traffic and to confirm latency/cost tradeoffs for a dedicted vs hosted config.
topics: A/B comparison UI and pairwise evaluation
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, happy to see the Talon crew — we've got about 50 minutes, we'll walk through EvalOps, show prompt-set workflows, reg alerts, and an A/B compare. Luca will do the console demo and Jordan will jump into the backend bits.
[00:18] Priya Das: Thanks, Maya. We're primarily concerned about silent regressions after model updates — we had a drift incident last quarter — so want something that can catch subtle prompt-level degradations. Also curious about cost/latency tradeoffs.
[00:32] Luca Ortiz: Totally. At a high level, Redwood's EvalOps ties prompt sets (we call them 'scenarios') to continuous monitoring. You can attach golden responses, define metrics (e.g. BLEU-ish, exact match, custom regex), and then the console surfaces both trending drift and sudden regressions.
[00:48] Evan Murray: Quick question — does that work for streaming APIs and async batch both? Our pipeline uses both real-time chat and nightly batch scoring.
[01:02] Jordan Park: Yes, we capture token-level timestamps for streaming, and batch runs can be scheduled or kicked off via API. The same eval harness runs locally or in our hosted runner.
[01:18] Sofia Alvarez: When you say "alerts" what are the channels? Pager? Slack? Email?
[01:24] Maya Chen: Configurable — Slack, PagerDuty, webhooks, and we can push summary reports to S3/GCS. You can also configure severity thresholds and automatic rollbacks to a fallback model.
[01:36] Aaron Li: Rollback — hmm — do you do automatic traffic shifting on failure? That's a hard ask for us.
[01:44] Luca Ortiz: It's opt-in. The rollout policies support canary, A/B, and failover rules. Automatic shift can be enabled for non-critical paths, but customers usually want manual approval for high-stakes flows.
[01:59] [00:60] Priya Das: Sorry quick note — we need proof of SOC 2 controls and KMS integration because finance regs.
[02:06] Maya Chen: Understood — we'll attach our SOC2 summary and KMS docs. Redwood Private supports VPC and customer-managed keys.
[02:14] Aaron Li: Are audit logs queryable? We need to show prompt-level provenance.
[02:20] Jordan Park: Yes, we store request/response hashes, eval results, and metadata with timestamps. We can export logs to your SIEM.
[02:28] [02:30] Luca Ortiz: Okay cool, let's jump into the console. I'm sharing my screen — this is the EvalOps tab. At the top: prompt sets, metrics, and active experiments.
[02:46] Luca Ortiz: Here I've loaded an example "credit-decision" prompt set. Each scenario shows baseline metrics, historical trends, and recent anomalous scores. The heatmap highlights where the model started deviating.
[03:05] Sofia Alvarez: That heatmap's useful — can we group scenarios by user intent or product area?
[03:12] Luca Ortiz: Yes, tags and folders — you can create groups and attach teams. You can also pin scenarios to a dashboard.
[03:21] [03:30] Priya Das: Walk me through an alert event — what does it look like?
[03:35] Luca Ortiz: Here's an example. The system detected a 14% drop in our custom satisfaction score after a model rollout. We surfaced pairwise diffs (A vs B) and highlighted failing examples. You can click into the pairwise view and run side-by-side comparisons with tokens, logits, and classification deltas.
[03:56] Aaron Li: Are the pairwise scores deterministic? We need reproducible comparisons.
[04:02] Jordan Park: We capture seed and model config. For deterministic runs you can pin the same sampling settings. Also the console saves the exact model variant and quantization profile.
[04:14] [04:30] Evan Murray: About A/B: can we do statistical significance tests inside the console? Like bootstrap / t-test?
[04:38] Luca Ortiz: We provide built-in significance tests and bootstrap confidence intervals; you can also export raw per-example scores and run custom analysis.
[04:49] Priya Das: Nice. For our compliance team we'll need exportable PDFs of the A/B report.
[04:56] Maya Chen: Yep, exportable reports and audit trails available.
[05:03] [05:20] Luca Ortiz: Now the Optimize tab — this is where we recommend batching configs and quantization profiles based on your workload. For example, we might recommend int8 QAT or 4-bit quant on certain models to reduce cost by ~2-4x while keeping your eval metrics within tolerance.
[05:38] Priya Das: How do you define "within tolerance"? Is that based on our golden metrics?
[05:43] Luca Ortiz: Exactly—Optimize runs a sensitivity analysis across prompt sets and reports estimated delta in your chosen metrics. You set an SLO window, e.g., max 3% drop in satisfaction, and Optimize filters recommendations that meet that constraint.
[05:58] Aaron Li: Any risk of catastrophic failures with quant? We worry about hallucinations increasing.
[06:05] Jordan Park: We recommend per-workload evals. In the console you can run a quantization sweep and see per-scenario deltas; if a scenario's quality regresses beyond the tolerated threshold we mark it as disqualified for that profile.
[06:20] [06:30] Evan Murray: Latency numbers — do you show p95/p99 by model variant? We need that for SLOs.
[06:36] Luca Ortiz: Yes, per-model and per-route p50/p95/p99 are shown with cost per token. We also provide token-level cost breakdowns.
[06:48] Priya Das: On infrastructure, would you recommend Hosted or Dedicated for us? Our throughput is moderate but we need predictable latency and data isolation.
[06:58] Maya Chen: For predictable latency and data isolation we'd generally start with Dedicated — reserved pools — if you need strict data residency and KMS, Private is the option. Hosted is easiest to start and cheaper for low volume, but Dedicated gives stronger latency SLAs.
[07:12] Aaron Li: What's the typical time to provision Dedicated?
[07:16] Jordan Park: We can spin up a dev Dedicated pool in 7–10 business days for common GPU types; enterprise provisioning with VPC peering takes longer.
[07:26] [07:30] Priya Das: Can we run the pilot with Hosted first and then switch to Dedicated mid-pilot? We want to validate detection before committing to reserved capacity.
[07:38] Luca Ortiz: Yes, the API and console are consistent across modes; you can run the pilot on Hosted and then flip routing to Dedicated when ready. The rollouts preserve model versions and ids.
[07:50] Sofia Alvarez: For the A/B workflow, can product owners create experiments or do we need SE involvement?
[07:57] Maya Chen: The console is self-serve for experiment creation, but SEs help with metric definitions and check the eval harness. You can set guardrails so product owners can't change rollout policies without approvals.
[08:10] [08:20] Evan Murray: Security again: do you support SSO + RBAC? We're on Okta.
[08:24] Jordan Park: Yes — SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and role-based access control. Also field-level redaction for logs if needed.
[08:34] Priya Das: Earlier you mentioned "prefix caching" — will that affect our latency numbers if we cache certain prompts?
[08:41] Luca Ortiz: Automatic prefix/KV caching can reduce repeat-token latency significantly for deterministic prompts. We show cache hit rates and you'll see cost benefit rolled into Optimize recommendations.
[08:52] [09:00] Maya Chen: Quick demo of running a pairwise comparison — I'm initiating a run comparing model-v1 vs model-v2 using Talon's credit prompts. Starting... you'll see it run through the prompt set and compute per-scenario metrics.
[09:16] Aaron Li: Seeing results — there's a cluster of failures around the income-normalization scenario.
[09:20] Luca Ortiz: Right — you can open those failing examples; the console annotates differences and suggests potential prompt edits. We can also auto-generate a small regression test to run on deploy.
[09:33] Priya Das: Can the system run continuous regression checks against production traffic with sampling?
[09:39] Jordan Park: Yes, we support live sampling — you can route a percent of real traffic to a shadow eval path and compute metrics without affecting users.
[09:46] [09:60] Evan Murray: About data retention — we need 7 years for audit purposes, is that supported?
[10:02] Jordan Park: We offer configurable retention; longer retention is an enterprise add-on and can be exported to your storage.
[10:10] Sofia Alvarez: On the eval template — can we define multi-turn scenarios with expected state transitions?
[10:16] Luca Ortiz: Absolutely — scenarios support multi-turn chains with session state and you can assert on final state or intermediate responses.
[10:26] Priya Das: OK, quick item — we have a legal review that will want to see DPA + subprocessor list.
[10:31] Maya Chen: We'll include DPA and subprocessor details in the packet we send after this call.
[10:36] [10:40] Aaron Li: One more technical — do you store raw prompts and responses internally? Our compliance needs to redact PII.
[10:44] Jordan Park: We can redact or hash raw content on ingest; customers can enable field redaction and only store hashes and metadata.
[10:52] Maya Chen: Cool. Time check — about 15 minutes left. Let's talk pilot scope. We're proposing a 4-week pilot: week 0 import prompts & baseline run, week 1 smoke A/B and quant sweeps, week 2 production shadow sampling + alerts tuning, week 3 handoff and final report. Success criteria: detect at least one regression or demonstrate <3% delta under recommended quant profile, and p95 latency below X ms for your SLAs.
[11:25] Priya Das: That sounds workable — we'll need to confirm internal stakeholders and approvals.
[11:30] Sofia Alvarez: What does the pricing for the pilot look like?
[11:33] Maya Chen: Pilot pricing is waived for 2 weeks; longer pilots have a nominal fee — for Dedicated pricing we'll share the reserved capacity tiers. I'll send a quote.
[11:42] [11:50] Aaron Li: Will you be able to run the benchmark on our dataset? We have some protected fields — can you run it in a way that doesn't touch sensitive data?
[11:56] Jordan Park: We can run on hashed/obfuscated data or provide a self-hosted runner you can run inside your VPC and share aggregated metrics back to us.
[12:06] Priya Das: Good. One last question — competitors. We've evaluated Anthropic's dashboard and a few OSS toolkits; how is Redwood differentiating on EvalOps?
[12:14] Luca Ortiz: Two big things: 1) unified stack across hosted/dedicated/private deployments so you don't rewrite evals; 2) Optimize recommendation engine ties QoS metrics to cost-optimizations — so you get actionable quant/batch profiles that are provably within your tolerances.
[12:31] Maya Chen: Also our rollout policies are tightly integrated with alerts — automatic canaries + pairwise diffs make root cause faster.
[12:38] [12:45] Priya Das: Great. I think we have a clear path.
[12:48] Maya Chen: Awesome — we'll follow up with the packet: SOC2, DPA, Eval template, and a pricing quote. Luca will provision the trial workspace and we'll schedule the kickoff.
[12:58] Evan Murray: Thanks all.
[13:00] Maya Chen: Thanks, everyone — we'll send next steps.
[13:04] [END]
